artworks.title: Cassandra
artworks.description: Oil painting by the English Pre-Raphaelite painter Evelyn De Morgan, in the collection of the De Morgan Foundation. The prophetess tears at her flame-red hair before the burning city of Troy — cursed by Apollo to foresee the catastrophe and never to be believed, she stands helpless as everything she foretold comes true.

artworks.title: Ajax and Cassandra
artworks.description: Large oil painting by the British artist Solomon Joseph Solomon, now in the Art Gallery of Ballarat, Australia. During the sack of Troy, Ajax the Locrian tears Cassandra from the sanctuary of Athena where she had clung to the goddess's image — the sacrilege for which, the mythographers tell, the lesser Ajax earned divine wrath.

artworks.title: Cassandra
artworks.description: Head of Cassandra by the Pre-Raphaelite artist Anthony Frederick Augustus Sandys, dated 1885. Caught at the moment of prophecy, she cries out with wide eyes, her hair and white drapery streaming against the walls of Troy — a vision of warnings fated to go unheeded.

films.title: The Trojan Women
films.description: Geneviève Bujold's Cassandra is Euripides' prophetess unbound — cursed to see the truth and never be believed, still crying the fall while the Greeks divide the captives.

films.title: Troy: Fall of a City
films.description: The BBC/Netflix retelling keeps Cassandra's ignored warnings in the palace — Apollo's curse as the voice nobody in Troy will hear.

films.title: Helen of Troy
films.description: Wise's epic gives Cassandra her traditional role at the horse: the prophetess who sees the trap and is dragged from Athena's altar for saying so.

films.title: Helen of Troy
films.description: The USA Network miniseries opens on Cassandra's prophecy about Paris — the sister whose warnings Priam will not heed until the city burns.

films.title: The Trojan Horse
films.description: Lidia Alfonsi's Cassandra stands among Ferroni's Trojan court — the prophetess in a peplum Iliad built around Aeneas and the horse.

music.title: Les Troyens
music.description: Berlioz makes Cassandra the tragic engine of Acts I–II: she foresees the horse, the fire, and her own death — and Troy still will not listen.

music.title: Oresteia
music.description: Taneyev's musical trilogy gives Cassandra her Aeschylean role — the captive who prophesies Agamemnon's murder and walks into her own.

music.title: Agamemnon
music.description: Werder's twelve-tone setting of Aeschylus keeps Cassandra on stage as soprano — the Trojan voice that Argos cannot understand.

music.title: King Priam
music.description: Tippett's Iliad opera stations Cassandra among Troy's doomed house — the prophetess as witness to Priam's choices and the city's fall.

popCulture.title: Cassandra
popCulture.creator: Christa Wolf
popCulture.description: Wolf's Kassandra retells the fall of Troy from the prophetess's stream of consciousness — Apollo's curse as an East German parable of unheeded truth.

popCulture.title: The Firebrand
popCulture.creator: Marion Zimmer Bradley
popCulture.description: Bradley's Trojan War novel centres Kassandra as Amazon-trained priestess — the war retold through the sister who saw it coming.

popCulture.title: Cassandra (metaphor)
popCulture.description: English made the prophetess a byword for accurate warnings no one believes — any disregarded truth-teller still wears her name.

popCulture.title: A Thousand Ships
popCulture.creator: Natalie Haynes
popCulture.description: Haynes gives Cassandra a chapter among the Trojan women — the ignored voice woven into a chorus of those the epics sidelined.
